title: Banning data centers would blow up the U.S. economy
gist: Noah Smith documents a collapse in U.S. public support for data centers — from 43/42 for/against in Aug 2025 to 21/71 a year later, with local opposition now above the historic peak of anti-nuclear sentiment — and notes that Texas has joined New York in pausing construction, closing the red-state escape valve. He argues energy, not water, is the resource AI and humans genuinely compete for, and that a broad ban would remove what he calls the main engine of U.S. growth.

themes.theme: Data center opposition goes national and bipartisan

insights.claim: Support for building a data center nearby collapsed from 43% for / 42% against in August 2025 to 21% for / 71% against a year later, with 55% strongly opposed.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A ~22-point swing in twelve months is a permitting-risk repricing signal for anyone underwriting multi-year data center capex.
insights.quote: Today, just 21% said they support data center construction near them, while 71% are opposed
insights.locator: An August 2025 survey conducted by Embold Research

insights.claim: Opposition to local data center construction at 71% now exceeds the all-time peak of U.S. opposition to nuclear power plant construction, which topped out at 63% in 2001.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The nuclear comparison is the tell: this level of NIMBY sentiment historically precedes decade-long construction freezes.
insights.quote: was higher than the zenith of the opposition to the construction of nuclear power plants, which topped out at 63% in 2001
insights.locator: A Gallup poll released in May

insights.claim: Marquette Law School polling shows 71% of voters nationwide believe data center costs outweigh benefits, and voters call AI development bad for society by 65%-35%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Public opinion on AI itself, not just its buildings, has turned decisively negative — raising political risk for the whole AI complex.
insights.quote: A survey from Marquette Law School found 71% of voters nationwide said the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits, while 29% said the reverse.
insights.locator: A survey from Marquette Law School

insights.claim: A YouGov poll for The Economist found only 23% of voters think data centers are good for the country against 48% who think they are bad, and 60% oppose one in their own community.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cross-pollster consistency means this is a stable structural preference, not a polling artifact.
insights.quote: A YouGov poll taken for The Economist found just 23% of voters who said the construction of data centers are good for the country, while 48% said they are bad for the country.
insights.locator: A YouGov poll taken for The Economist

insights.claim: New York imposed a data center moratorium in July 2026 and Texas followed in August, breaking the usual pattern where blocked blue-state industry simply relocates to red states.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Texas was the release valve; losing it removes the geographic arbitrage that made state-level bans economically irrelevant.
insights.quote: New York put a moratorium on data center construction in July, while Texas followed suit earlier this month.

insights.claim: There is still no strong federal data center pause and the bills introduced in Congress are mild, making federal escalation the key unhedged tail risk rather than a current fact.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Watch federal legislative language as the single binary that converts a state-level nuisance into a systemic AI capex shock.
insights.locator: So far, there has been no strong move

insights.claim: Data center opposition has become such a consensus middle-of-the-road position that a candidate's supporters would rather campaign on it than defend her cultural stances.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Anti-data-center is now the safe political position — meaning politicians of both parties face rising incentives to adopt it.
insights.locator: It’s pretty amazing that a pause on data center construction

themes.theme: Energy, not water, is the real scarcity

insights.claim: Data centers already account for more than 7% of U.S. electricity usage and that share appears to be on an exponential growth path, projected to surpass household uses like air conditioning, lighting and refrigeration within years.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Core datapoint for the power-demand trade: utilities, generation, transmission and grid equipment all key off this curve continuing.
insights.quote: Data centers already account for more than 7% of U.S. electricity usage, and the percentage appears to be on an exponential growth path.
insights.locator: But the energy concern is very real

insights.claim: The AI water controversy is essentially unfounded because data center cooling water is recycled continuously, with only a small evaporative loss needing replacement.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The most emotionally potent objection to data centers is factually weak — useful for handicapping which lawsuits and ordinances actually survive scrutiny.
insights.quote: Basically, data centers are just using that same water over and over again.
insights.locator: The reason, of course, is that the water

insights.claim: Voters cite water usage (18%), energy consumption (18%) and higher utility bills (15%) as their reasons for opposing data centers, and 38% say data centers are mostly bad for home energy costs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Retail electricity bills are the transmission channel from AI capex to political backlash; rate cases are the thing to monitor.
insights.quote: Respondents [to Gallup] said they opposed data center construction because of water usage (18%), energy consumption (18%) and higher utility bills (15%)
insights.locator: Resource use consistently ranks at the top

themes.theme: Comparative advantage and the resource-competition thesis

insights.claim: The real AI danger is not that humans become obsolete but that they become too expensive to sustain, because AI's owners bid up the price of the resources humans need to live.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes AI risk from unemployment to input-cost inflation — a very different set of hedges (energy, food, real assets) than a labor-displacement thesis implies.
insights.quote: the real danger isn’t that AI will render humans obsolete; the danger is that AI will render humans too expensive to sustain
insights.locator: So as I explained in my post

insights.claim: Comparative advantage protects human employment only when constraints are producer-specific: compute is specific to AI, but energy is not, so energy is where AI and humans directly compete.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: This is the analytical crux for long-horizon energy demand: AI's marginal willingness to pay for power is effectively unbounded if compute scales with energy.
insights.quote: Recall that comparative advantage prevails when there are producer-specific constraints. Compute is a constraint that’s specific to AI. Energy is not.

insights.claim: If additional compute can be manufactured simply by adding energy, market logic could make it economically rational to starve humans in order to generate more AI.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The extreme version of the energy-competition thesis; it is the stated justification for reserving resources for human use, i.e. hard caps on AI power draw.
insights.quote: If you can create more compute by simply putting more energy into the process, it could make economic sense to starve human beings in order to generate more and more AI.

insights.claim: Historical precedents for market-driven resource diversion away from locals include agribusiness consuming most Colorado River water during household shortages and cash-crop cultivation exacerbating late-1800s Indian famines that killed millions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supplies the historical base rate for the claim that price mechanisms can starve local populations of resources — grounding for resource-reservation policy.
insights.locator: In fact, things a little bit like this have happened before

insights.claim: The two defenses against AI outcompeting humans for resources are redistributing AI income to humans or reserving a fixed pool of natural resources for exclusively human use.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Anticipates the policy menu: expect either AI windfall taxes or hard energy set-asides, both of which cap AI margins.
insights.locator: There are a couple of obvious ways to guard

themes.theme: Macro risk from killing the AI buildout

insights.claim: Data center construction is the main engine of current U.S. growth, so a broad ban would throw Americans out of work and put a hole in retirement savings.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the AI capex cycle as the load-bearing component of both GDP and equity-linked household wealth — a policy shock here hits growth and portfolios simultaneously.
insights.quote: The big danger is that data center bans will choke off the main engine of U.S. growth, throwing a lot of Americans out of their jobs and putting a hole in Americans’ retirement savings.
insights.locator: The big danger is that data center bans

insights.claim: The author holds the split view that limiting physical resources devoted to AI is right in the long run but would clobber an already-wobbly U.S. economy in the short run.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The timing asymmetry is the trade: near-term restriction is a growth shock even if it is correct policy over a decade.
insights.quote: In the long run, I think limiting the physical resources devoted to AI would be a good thing; in the short run, it will simply clobber the already-wobbly U.S. economy.
insights.locator: Except now Texas is pausing data centers too

insights.claim: The physical location of data centers is irrelevant to AI progress itself, so scattered state bans slow local economic activity without slowing AI capability — which is why near-universal or federal bans are the only ones that matter.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Distinguishes political noise from actual capability risk: only near-total geographic closure changes the AI trajectory.
insights.locator: Nor would a few state-level bans affect the progress of AI
